title: Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) Dataset: Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Bridging Communication Barrier among the Deaf Learners
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the communication barriers faced by deaf learners in Kenya, especially the difficulty of translating between spoken/written English and Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) in educational settings. The authors argue that limited sign language access, few interpreters, and the mismatch between English and KSL contribute to reduced inclusion and learning opportunities for deaf students.

The study focuses on building an AI-oriented KSL dataset rather than evaluating a finished classroom intervention. The dataset includes English sentences, KSL glosses, signed video recordings, and HamNoSys transcriptions. Data were collected from teachers/tutors of deaf learners and deaf learners across Kenyan deaf schools and a tertiary technical training institution. The work uses mixed methods within an experimental design for the dataset development process, including sentence generation, video recording, segmentation, and transcription.

The population includes deaf learners from early childhood through primary, secondary, and tertiary contexts, along with teachers and sign-language teacher trainees. The paper reports approximately 14,000 English sentences with corresponding KSL gloss, about 20,000 KSL videos, and 4,000 transcribed words. The main conclusion is that the dataset can support future AI tools for translating English to KSL and thereby help bridge communication barriers and promote inclusion in education and beyond.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive mixed-methods project paper about dataset construction, not an experimental evaluation of an intervention’s effects on learner outcomes. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically described, but there is no causal comparison or outcome estimation, so evidence strength is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional value for deaf inclusion and future assistive technology development, but it does not report measured educational impact or effect sizes. The likely impact is promising but currently unclear because it is a foundational resource-building study rather than an outcomes study.

interventions.use_case: Creation of an AI4KSL assistive technology dataset for spoken English to Kenyan Sign Language translation, including glossing, video segmentation, and HamNoSys transcription to support future real-time sign-language rendering.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the AI4KSL dataset is intended to reduce communication barriers for deaf learners and support wider inclusion in education and other sectors. The study produced about 14,000 English sentences with KSL gloss, about 20,000 signed KSL videos, and 4,000 HamNoSys transcriptions, but it does not evaluate downstream learning effects or provide effect sizes.
finding.measure: Dataset creation outputs and intended institutional/inclusion value
finding.study_size: n=48 teachers/tutors and n=400 deaf learners; dataset outputs from 14,000 sentences, 20,000 videos, 4,000 transcriptions

finding.finding_summary: The work reports a structured pipeline for collecting, glossing, splitting, segmenting, and transcribing sign-language data that can support future machine translation and sign-language tooling. No quantitative efficiency gains are measured, but the dataset infrastructure is presented as a resource to streamline development of assistive sign-language applications.
finding.measure: Dataset production process and transcription workflow
finding.study_size: n=48 teachers/tutors and n=400 deaf learners
